۱:۱۰:۳۳روی ما بحث داغ مهاجرت است و درس نهم کتاب به همین موضوع می‌پردازد: مهاجرت. برای روشن شدن موضوع، مهاجرت را به‌عنوان قراردادی با سه شرط پایه بررسی می‌کنیم. شرط اول این است که میزبان اجازهٔ ورود به مهاجران بدهد. شرط دوم این است که در ازای آن، مهاجران دست‌کم هنجارها و ارزش‌های اصلی کشور میزبان را بپذیرند، حتی اگر به معنای کنار گذاشتن برخی هنجارها و ارزش‌های سنتی خودشان باشد. شرط سوم این است که اگر مهاجران به اندازهٔ کافی ادغام شوند، سرانجام اعضای برابرحقوق کشور میزبان می‌شوند؛ یعنی «آن‌ها» به «ما» تبدیل می‌شوند. این سه شرط پایهٔ مهاجرت را در نظر بگیریم و کوتاه دربارهٔ هرکدام حرف بزنیم. بند اول قرارداد

۱:۱۱:۳۰مهاجرت می‌گوید میزبان باید اجازهٔ ورود به مهاجران بدهد؛ اما این وظیفه است یا لطف؟ هواداران مهاجرت معتقدند کشورها وظیفهٔ اخلاقی دارند نه‌تنها پناهجویان، بلکه مردم کشورهای بسیار فقیر را که دنبال کار و آیندهٔ بهتری‌اند بپذیرند. آن‌ها باور دارند در جهانی یکپارچه همهٔ انسان‌ها در برابر هم تعهدات اخلاقی دارند و کسانی که چنین حس مسئولیتی ندارند خودخواه و حتی نژادپرست‌اند. در مقابل، مخالفان مهاجرت معتقدند یکی از بنیادی‌ترین حقوق هر جمع انسانی، چه یک ارتش باشد چه جامعه‌ای از مهاجران، محافظت از خود در برابر تجاوز است. پس با این دیدگاه، اگر رأی‌دهندگان سوئدی تصمیم بگیرند

۱:۱۲:۲۶که دیگر مهاجر سوری نمی‌خواهند، حق دارند جلوی ورودشان را بگیرند؛ و اگر سوئدی‌ها آن‌ها را بپذیرند، باید صرفاً نشانهٔ لطفشان دیده شود. آنچه موضوع را پیچیده می‌کند این است که در بسیاری موارد مردم هم خدا را می‌خواهند و هم خرما را! کشورهای زیادی هستند که نسبت به مهاجران غیرقانونی حساسیتی نشان نمی‌دهند یا حتی کارگر خارجی را موقت می‌پذیرند. چرا؟ چون می‌خواهند از نیروی کار ارزان استفاده کنند. اما وقتی به آن‌ها می‌گویید این مهاجران غیرقانونی که کار و زحمت می‌کشند باید بتوانند قانونی مهاجرت کنند و حق شهروندی داشته باشند، می‌گویند: «نه، ما مهاجر نمی‌خواهیم.» برای مثالی خارج از کتاب، دقیقاً همان اتفاقی که در ایران دربارهٔ

۱:۱۳:۲۱مهاجران افغانستانی می‌افتد همین است. از نیروی کار ارزان افغانستانی‌ها در همهٔ زمینه‌ها استفاده می‌کنیم، اما هم‌زمان می‌گوییم مهاجر افغانستانی نمی‌خواهیم. این موضوع در درازمدت می‌تواند به جوامعی سلسله‌مراتبی بینجامد که طبقات بالا حقوق کامل شهروندی دارند و از مهاجران خارجی بهره‌کشی می‌کنند؛ همان‌طور که همین حالا در قطر، دبی و بسیاری کشورهای دیگر می‌کنند. این بحث شرط اول مهاجرت بود. شرط دوم مهاجرت می‌گفت اگر مهاجران پذیرفته شوند، موظف‌اند در فرهنگ محلی ادغام شوند. اما حد این ادغام کجاست؟ اگر مهاجران از کشوری عمیقاً مذهبی بیایند، آیا باید جهان‌بینی سکولار را بپذیرند؟ آیا باید

۱:۱۴:۱۷الگوهای سنتی پوشش و تابوهای قضایی خودشان را کنار بگذارند؟ هواداران مهاجرت معتقدند مثلاً نباید مهاجران اروپا را وادار کرد با هویت اروپایی همرنگ شوند. باور دارند اگر اروپا چیزی به نام ارزش دارد، آن ارزش آزادی‌اش است؛ پس مهاجران هم باید در همهٔ زمینه‌ها حق انتخاب داشته باشند و آزاد باشند. در مقابل، مخالفان مهاجرت می‌پذیرند که آزادی یکی از مهم‌ترین ارزش‌های اروپاست، اما مهاجران را متهم می‌کنند که خودشان همین آزادی را زیر سؤال می‌برند. می‌گویند مهاجران زن‌ستیزند، بر خانواده‌شان سلطه دارند، در دین افراطی‌اند، و اگر اروپا همچنان از خاورمیانه مهاجر بپذیرد، به‌زودی به خاورمیانهٔ دوم تبدیل می‌شود. این بحثی پیچیده است

۱:۱۵:۱۴و شاید بخشی از این مشکل حل شود اگر مهاجران نشان دهند در دیدگاه‌هایشان دربارهٔ جنسیت و سیاست لیبرال و گشاده‌فکرند، و نه آن‌طور که مخالفان ادعا می‌کنند. و حالا بحث سوم؛ بند سوم قرارداد مهاجرت می‌گفت اگر مهاجران صادقانه برای ادغام تلاش کنند، کشور میزبان متعهد می‌شود آن‌ها را شهروند درجه‌یک بپذیرد. اما پرسش این است که دقیقاً چه زمانی لازم است مهاجران اعضای واقعی جامعه شناخته شوند؟

۱:۱۵:۵۳آیا مهاجران الجزایری نسل اول باید ناراحت باشند اگر پس از ۲۰ سال زندگی در فرانسه کاملاً فرانسوی شناخته نشوند؟ یا مهاجران نسل سومی که پدربزرگ و مادربزرگشان در دههٔ ۱۹۷۰ به فرانسه آمدند چطور؟ آیا هنوز مهاجرند، یا پس از سه نسل باید شهروند درجه‌یک شمرده شوند؟ هواداران مهاجرت انتظار دارند مهاجران زود به‌عنوان شهروند پذیرفته شوند، در حالی که مخالفان مهاجرت دورهٔ آزمایشی بسیار طولانی‌ای می‌خواهند.

۱:۱۶:۳۱مشکل اصلی این بحث شکاف میان زمان‌بندی فردی و زمان‌بندی جمعی است. از منظر جمعی، ۴۰ سال زمان بسیار کوتاهی است. پذیرش کامل گروه‌های خارجی از سوی یک جامعه در چند دهه انتظار نامعقولی است. تمدن‌های گذشته‌ای که بیگانگان را شهروند برابر پذیرفتند، مثل امپراتوری روم، خلافت اسلامی، امپراتوری چین و ایالات متحده، همه برای این دگرگونی به قرن‌ها، نه دهه‌ها، نیاز داشتند. اما خب، همین ۴۰ سال از منظر یک فرد می‌تواند یک عمر باشد. برای نوجوانی که پس از مهاجرت پدرش از الجزایر در فرانسه به دنیا آمده، به جای عربی فرانسوی حرف می‌زند و هرگز

۱:۱۷:۲۵الجزایر را ندیده، فرانسه تنها خانه‌ای است که می‌شناسد؛ و ۴۰ سال زمان بسیار درازی برای انتظار پذیرفته شدن است. این سه بحث و چالش را مطرح کردیم؛ اما بالاتر از همهٔ این اختلاف‌ها دربارهٔ تعریف دقیق قرارداد مهاجرت، پرسش نهایی این است که آیا هر دو طرف واقعاً به تعهداتشان در مهاجرت پایبندند یا نه؟ اصلاً قصد دارند آن سه شرط را برآورده کنند؟ مخالفان مهاجرت استدلال می‌کنند که مهاجران شرط دوم را برآورده نمی‌کنند؛ یعنی صادقانه برای ادغام تلاش نمی‌کنند و بسیاری‌شان دیدگاه‌های واپس‌گرایانه دارند.

۱:۱۸:۰۸بنابراین کشور میزبان دلیلی ندارد شرط سوم، یعنی به رسمیت شناختن آن‌ها به‌عنوان شهروند برابر، را برآورده کند. در پاسخ، هواداران مهاجرت می‌گویند این کشور میزبان است که به تعهدش در قرارداد عمل نمی‌کند. کشورهای میزبان با وجود تلاش صادقانهٔ اکثریت بزرگ مهاجران شرایط ادغام را دشوار می‌کنند و بدتر اینکه حتی با مهاجران نسل دوم و سومی که با موفقیت ادغام شده‌اند همچنان مثل شهروند درجه‌دو رفتار می‌کنند.

۱:۱۸:۵۰نکتهٔ ظریف بعدی این است: اگر ۱ میلیون مهاجر شهروندان قانون‌مداری باشند، اما ۱۰۰ نفر به گروه‌های تروریستی بپیوندند و به کشور میزبان حمله کنند، آیا یعنی کل جمعیت مهاجر به قرارداد پایبند نبوده و آن را نقض کرده است؟ برعکس، اگر مهاجری ۱۰۰ بار از خیابانی بگذرد و آزاری نبیند، اما یک بار یک نژادپرست به او حمله کند، آیا یعنی بومیان مهاجران را نپذیرفته‌اند؟ در بحث و نتیجه‌گیری دربارهٔ مهاجرت باید به این نکته‌ها هم خیلی توجه کنیم. اما زیر همهٔ این بحث‌ها پرسشی بسیار بنیادی‌تر پنهان است که به فهم ما از فرهنگ انسانی مربوط می‌شود. پرسش این است: آیا ممکن است،

۱:۱۹:۴۷مثلاً وقتی آلمانی‌ها دربارهٔ پذیرش ۱ میلیون پناهجوی سوری بحث می‌کنند، حق داشته باشند فکر کنند فرهنگ آلمانی به نحوی از فرهنگ سوری بهتر است؟ به زبان ساده، آیا یک آلمانی حق دارد فرهنگش را برتر از فرهنگ سوری بداند یا نه؟ برای پاسخ به این پرسش نگاهی به گذشته بیندازیم. ۱۰۰ سال پیش اروپایی‌ها مسلم می‌دانستند که برخی نژادها، به‌ویژه نژاد سفید، ذاتاً از نژادهای دیگر برترند. بعدها، پس از جنگ جهانی دوم و شکست فاشیست‌ها، نژادپرستی محکوم و از نظر اخلاقی هولناک معرفی شد. اما با گذشت زمان، نژادپرستی جایش را به «فرهنگ‌گرایی» داد؛ با چند تفاوت.

۱:۲۰:۴۱نژادپرستی سنتی سخت بر نظریه‌های زیستی تکیه داشت. در اوایل قرن بیستم در کشورهایی مثل بریتانیا، استرالیا و آمریکا به‌طور گسترده باور داشتند که برخی ویژگی‌های زیستیِ ارثی آفریقایی‌ها و چینی‌ها را کم‌هوش‌تر، کم‌نوآورتر و از نظر اخلاقی پست‌تر از اروپایی‌ها می‌کند؛ انگار مشکل در خونشان بود. آن نظریه‌ها زمانی اعتبار سیاسی و علمی چشمگیری داشتند، اما با پیشرفت علم اعتبارشان را از دست دادند و این بار هوادارانشان به فرهنگ روی آوردند. دوران ادعای اینکه سیاه‌پوستان به خاطر ژن‌های معیوب جرم می‌کنند گذشته، اما به جایش حالا ادعا می‌شود که جرم می‌کنند چون به فرهنگ‌هایی ناکارآمد و پست تعلق دارند.

۱:۲۱:۳۹بخش تأسف‌بار این است که پیش‌تر نژادپرستان نمی‌توانستند سیاه‌پوستان را سرزنش کنند که چرا پوستشان را سفید نکرده‌اند؛ اما فرهنگ‌گرایان می‌توانند آفریقایی‌ها یا مسلمانان را متهم کنند که چرا هنجارها و ارزش‌های فرهنگی غربی را نپذیرفته‌اند، و دقیقاً همین کار را می‌کنند. بسیاری از ادعاهای فرهنگ‌گرایانه سه کاستی بزرگ دارند. کاستی اول این است که فرهنگ‌گرایان اغلب برتری محلی را با برتری عینی اشتباه می‌گیرند؛ یعنی اگر منطقه‌ای وضع بهتری دارد، لزوماً به این معنا نیست که فرهنگش بهتر است.

۱:۲۲:۱۶کاستی دوم را با مثالی توضیح می‌دهم. مثلاً گفتن اینکه «فرهنگ اسلامی بسیار خشن است» ادعایی بسیار مبهم است، چون اول باید تعریف کنیم منظور از فرهنگ اسلامی چیست. شبه‌جزیرهٔ عربستان در سپیده‌دم اسلام است؟ امپراتوری عثمانی در قرن شانزدهم؟ پاکستان و افغانستان در آغاز قرن بیست‌ویکم؟ اصلاً معیار این ادعا چیست؟ اگر امپراتوری عثمانی قرن شانزدهم را با اروپای غربی قرن شانزدهم مقایسه کنیم، به این نتیجه می‌رسیم که فرهنگ اسلامی در مقایسه با فرهنگ اروپای غربی خشن نیست؛ در واقع فرهنگ اروپای غربی خشن‌تر بود. اگر جلوتر بیاییم و افغانستانِ زیر حکومت طالبان را با، مثلاً، سوئیس امروز مقایسه کنیم، به نتیجهٔ دیگری می‌رسیم. پس نمی‌شود این‌قدر کلی حرف زد. اما سومین و

۱:۲۳:۱۲بزرگ‌ترین مشکل ادعاهای فرهنگ‌گرایانه این است که اغلب بر پیش‌داوری دربارهٔ افراد تکیه دارند. مثلاً چون کسی از ایران به کشوری اروپایی مهاجرت می‌کند، فرض می‌شود که چون ایرانی است حتماً مسلمان است، و بنابراین همهٔ کاستی‌هایی که در ذهنم به مسلمانان نسبت می‌دهم باید در این آدم هم باشد. در مجموع، بحث مهاجرت بحثی است میان دو موضع سیاسی مشروع که باید با روال‌های متعارف دموکراتیک حل شود و نباید به منازعه‌ای آشتی‌ناپذیر تبدیل شود. اگر ۵۰۰ میلیون اروپایی مرفه نتوانند چند میلیون پناهجوی فقیر و درمانده را در خود ادغام کنند، دیگر امیدی نمی‌ماند که بشر بر مشکلات بزرگ‌تر جامعهٔ جهانی چیره شود.

متن انگلیسی اصلی

Hello friends! I’m Amir Soudbakhsh, and on the "Rokh" YouTube channel, I share book summaries from time to time; books that are related to history in one way or another. In this episode, I’m going to share a summary of one of the best books I’ve read in the last few years; a book that deeply makes one think and reflect. The extraordinary book "21 Lessons for the 21st Century" by Yuval Noah Harari. "21 Lessons for the 21st Century" has also been published in Iran by Parseh Publications, translated by Ms. Soudabeh Gheisari. The author, Mr. Harari, is probably known to all of you , mostly for his book "Sapiens," and now, "21 Lessons for the 21st Century." This book was first published in 2018, and its subject is a comprehensive and precise exploration of the most important issues facing the world today and the near future of humanity. Given the staggering pace of technological advancement and the emergence of new capabilities that can be both beneficial and threatening, Harari addresses the challenges humans face in controlling their lives amidst the constant and sometimes confusing changes of modern life in this readable and engaging work. Let’s get into "21 Lessons for the 21st Century." In the introduction, the author, Mr. Harari, writes that his first book, "Sapiens," examined the human past and showed how an insignificant ape came to rule planet Earth. Moving forward, in this book, I contemplate the present time and place, focusing on the current dilemmas and the near future of human societies. So, "Sapiens" is about the human past, while this book is about the present and near future of humanity . What are the biggest challenges facing humans? What should we teach our children in this era? Is there a new war on the horizon or not? And which civilization dominates the world? What should be done regarding problems like unemployment, cultural nationalism, terrorism, and other issues? Without claiming to be exhaustive, this book attempts to address various aspects of these issues and problems. The book consists of 21 lessons in 5 parts; in the first episode, we will cover up to the beginning of the tenth lesson, which makes up the first two parts, and in the second episode, we will tell you about the next three parts, up to the end of the twenty-first lesson. As always, please note that I am narrating a summary here; the author's opinions and the topics raised in the book are not the result of our team's research. We try to present the concept and core of the book to you in summary; impartially and without adding or removing anything. First, the book provides a brief explanation about its various sections. The first part of the book begins by examining the difficult current political and technical state of the world, and then addresses the dangers that technology brings us; the title of this section is "The Technological Challenge." In the second part, titled "The Political Challenge," after outlining the challenges facing modern humans, a wide range of potential and probable responses is examined. For instance, can Facebook engineers use artificial intelligence to create a global community that can guarantee human freedom, or not? We should return to the sources of our ancient religious traditions and draw inspiration from them. In the third part, titled "Despair and Hope," we will see that although unprecedented and great challenges lie ahead and severe political divisions dominate the world, if humanity can overcome its fears and adopt a more humble stance toward its opinions, more opportunities will be gained. The fourth part, titled "Truth," poses the question of whether Homo sapiens is capable of giving meaning to the world it has created. And in the fifth and final part, titled "Resilience," different topics are raised: who we are, what we should do in life, and which skills we need. Given everything we know and do not know about science, and given the knowledge we have about God, politics, and religion, what can we say about the meaning of life today, among other topics. Well, with this introduction, let's move on to the first part called "The Technological Challenge," which contains 4 lessons. The title of the first lesson is "Disillusionment," and on its first page, next to the title, this sentence is written. Humanity has lost its belief in the liberal story that has dominated global politics over the recent decades. To enter the lesson , I will provide a very brief and introductory explanation about the concept of liberalism and liberal states for those who do not know. This explanation is outside the scope of the book. Liberalism means freedom-seeking, and liberal states are those where individual freedom is the most important political goal of the government. Liberal states support freedom of thought and freedom of speech. They speak of free markets and diverse global economies, and well, they have all sorts of different branches and theories that we will not delve into. Most European and United States governments are liberal states, and in this part, the book wants to talk about the flaws of liberal states, or as the author calls it, the liberal story. The author wants to compare the liberal story with the stories and ideologies of previous states like Communism and Fascism, examine its flaws, and see what happens in the end. Let's go to the book. During the twentieth century, global rulers in Berlin, Moscow, and New York formulated three grand stories: the Fascist story in Berlin, the Communist story in Moscow, and the Liberal story in New York and London. World War II destroyed the fascist story, then the communist story collapsed, and in the end, only the liberal story remained. Humans fought for freedom, and freedom captured fortresses step by step. Democratic governments replaced brutal dictatorships. However, alongside this, we know that everything in the world is not well and there are still many obstacles to overcome. Large parts of the globe are still under the control of dictators. Still, seemingly democratic governments question the independence of the judiciary, limit freedom of the press, and label any opponent as a traitor to the homeland. But the good thing is that we now know what to do to overcome these problems. More freedom for people. We must defend human rights. Give everyone the right to vote. Establish free markets and let people, ideas, and goods move across the world in the simplest way possible. This is exactly what the liberal story says. But is the liberal story good and complete enough to solve all our problems? Certainly not. People all over the world became increasingly disillusioned with the liberal story after the 2008 global financial crisis, and this disillusionment grew further in 2016 due to two major events. The first event was Brexit, or Britain's vote to leave the European Union, and the second was the rise of Donald Trump in the United States; events that fractured the global community. Many liberals fear that Brexit and the rise of Donald Trump signal the collapse of human civilization; the collapse of human civilization, especially after the emergence of a phenomenon called artificial intelligence. We are learning to design brains and prolong life, but no one knows what consequences await us. Humans have always been skilled at inventing tools but haven't had much luck in using those tools wisely. In the past, we humans gained the ability to transform the world around us and reshape the entire planet. But since we didn't understand the complexity of the global environment, we unknowingly disrupted the ecological system, and we are currently on the verge of an ecological collapse. A very important issue that gets no attention at all. In the early 1990s, some thinkers and politicians confidently claimed that all the major political and economic problems of the past had now been solved, and the repaired liberal system—consisting of democracy, human rights, free markets, and state welfare—was the ultimate solution we wanted and would solve everything; it seemed that this liberal system was set to remove all national borders and unite humanity into a single, free global society. So it seems that history is coming to an end. But no, history has not ended, and we must not forget that after the eras of Hitler and Stalin, we are now living in the era of Trump. While all the major movements of the twentieth century spoke of the integration of human groups and the formation of a global society. Donald Trump does not offer such a vision; on the contrary, his main message is that it is not America's duty to formulate and promote a global vision. Trump pursues a United States that separates itself from the global community and considers only its own interests. Most of those who voted for Trump and Brexit did not necessarily reject the liberal order and freedom. No. They have mainly lost their belief in the global dimension of liberalism. These people think that to preserve freedom, the best thing to do is to build a wall around their borders and apply illiberal policies toward foreigners while maintaining liberal policies for themselves, thus prioritizing "our people" and "our country" above all else. Governments also try to overshadow everything else by bringing up the issue of national security. If you look closely at Russian society, there is a very small group that monopolizes a vast portion of the country's wealth and power, using their control over the media to hide their illegal activities and strengthen their rule. Those who are known as oligarchs. The ruling oligarchy can blame others for its mistakes through its monopoly on the media and divert public attention toward foreign threats. Therefore, it constantly talks about guarding borders and national security. When you live under the rule of such an oligarchy, they always bring up a crisis or an issue to overshadow unpleasant problems like welfare services or environmental pollution. When a nation faces the danger of a foreign invasion, who has the time to worry about the pollution of rivers? A corrupt oligarch can extend his rule indefinitely by creating a wave of endless crises and presenting his country as a safe place for all the people of the world. But, in contrast to the countless people who dream of immigrating to liberal countries like Germany, Canada, or Australia, how many people dream of immigrating to Russia? What happened? We returned to liberal societies, that yes, humanity ultimately does not abandon the liberal story because it has no better option. However, with the discrediting of global communism and subsequently the decline in the credibility of global liberalism, humans have mistakenly thought that perhaps it is better to abandon the idea of a single global story altogether. Perhaps every country should adopt a different specific ideal and redefine it with its own ancient traditions. Something that some politicians are currently doing. Donald Trump, with the promise of making America great again, says we want to return to the old days. He wants an isolationist America that builds a wall between itself and its neighbors, prioritizing its own interests over all liberal principles. In Britain, Brexit proponents dream of turning Britain into an independent power as if they were still living in the Victorian era. Chinese rulers have redefined their indigenous imperial and Confucian legacies. In a way that suits them, of course. In Russia, Putin's official vision is the restoration of the old Tsarist Empire. Putin has vowed to bring back the former glory of the Tsars. Radical Islamists want to replicate the system Prophet Muhammad established in Medina 1,400 years ago, and Jewish fundamentalists in Israel go even further, dreaming of a return to 2,500 years ago, the dawn of Judaism. And well, the liberal leaders of the modern world look at such developments with horror, hoping humanity will return to the liberal path in time to prevent disaster. The liberal collective, despite its many flaws, has a much better track record than the other options. The reality is that most humans had never before experienced the relative peace and tranquility they enjoyed at the beginning of the twenty-first century under the liberal order. However, we must admit that even liberalism has no clear answer to the greatest problems we are facing. What are the greatest problems? Environmental collapse and technological disruption via artificial intelligence. Perhaps it is time to fully break free from the past and create a brand new story that goes beyond not only the old gods, nations, and ideologies, but even the modern values of freedom, equality, and liberalism. But we must not forget that before people accept a new story, they lose faith in the old ones, and this has led people into a period of nihilism and disillusionment. Disillusionment, which was also the title of the first of the book's 21 lessons. In the following chapters, the author attempts to explain some of the confusing possibilities facing us and offers solutions for their problems. Of course, it is a matter of possibilities and predictions. Because to escape humanity's predicaments in the near future, we need a better understanding of the challenges that technology is going to present us with. The information technology and biotechnology revolutions are still in their early stages. There is no doubt that the technological revolution will accelerate in the coming decades, putting humanity to the hardest tests it has ever faced. The technological revolution may soon push billions of people out of the labor market, creating a massive "useless" class, and with the onset of the crisis of unemployment, it may create such social and political tensions that no ideology will be able to control. The next lesson of the book is about this very subject. About work. Work is one of the greatest dilemmas facing humanity now and in the near future. As we mentioned , the title of the second chapter is " Work," and it says in the middle of the page that when you grow up, you will probably be unemployed. We don't know what the job market will look like in 2050, but we do know that every area of production will be transformed by AI and robotics. From yogurt production to teaching yoga. However, there is disagreement regarding the timing and the nature of this transformation. Some think that within just the next decade or two, billions of people will become economically redundant and useless. Others believe that in the long run, new job positions will be created and greater prosperity will be generated for everyone. This fear of automation, which is supposed to ultimately lead to unemployment, dates back to the nineteenth century. Back then, they also said that in the near future, factories would become automated, machines would replace workers, and everyone would be unemployed. But, well , that didn't happen. Although, we have good and valid reasons to think that today's era is different and that the problem of unemployment might grab humanity in the near future. Now, we will explain the reasons. Humans possess two types of abilities. Physical ability and cognitive ability; industrial machines in the past mainly competed with humans through purely physical abilities. While humans had a major superiority over machines in terms of cognition, and this cognitive ability helped them a lot. Physical labor decreased significantly, but tasks that required understanding and cognition increased, and new jobs were created. But the point is that now, humans not only cannot compete with the physical strength of robots, but our cognitive ability is also bowing down to artificial intelligence. AI can even be suitable for tasks that require insight and recognition. For example, it is predicted that by 2050, it will be possible for AI and robotics to create personal bodyguards and human-like psychiatrists. However, note that what we are facing in the near future is not the replacement of millions of human workers with millions of robots and computers, but rather a network of computers will likely replace human individuals. I will give an example so you understand better. When two vehicles reach a common intersection at the same time, the drivers might make a mistake in judgment and collide. But all autonomous driverless cars in the near future can communicate with each other, and when two driverless cars reach a common intersection, they are not actually two separate units but parts of a single algorithm. For this reason, the possibility of an accident becomes much lower, near zero. Furthermore, if the Minister of Transportation decides to add a clause to traffic regulations or change driving laws, all driverless vehicles can be easily updated, and all of them will follow the new rule exactly. So, two important non-human capabilities of artificial intelligence are its capacity for vast connectivity with millions of machines simultaneously and its ability to update in real-time. These advantages are so significant that in many professional fields, it is more sensible for humans to step aside and give their place to a collection of computers and robots. Currently, millions of people lose their lives annually in traffic accidents, and over 90 percent of these accidents are due to human error. It is expected that replacing human drivers with computers could reduce road fatalities and injuries by up to 90 percent. In other words, the use of autonomous vehicles could potentially save a million lives each year. One million people is a very large number. Thus, halting automation and artificial intelligence in areas like transportation and healthcare, simply to preserve human job positions, could be madness; because what must ultimately be preserved are humans, not job positions. Of course, the loss of traditional jobs in any field, from art to healthcare, can be partially compensated for by the creation of new jobs or focusing on other occupations. For example, general practitioners who focus on diagnosing known diseases may soon give their place to artificial intelligence. But this way, we will have more financial resources, allowing us to invest in human doctors to conduct more research and create new drugs or surgical methods. The problem, however, is that such jobs likely require a high level of expertise, and for this reason, the problem of unskilled unemployed workers will not be solved. Consequently, despite the emergence of many new human job positions, we will likely witness the rise of a new "useless" class. The people who were carriage drivers in the nineteenth century are today's taxi drivers. But perhaps the professional future for many will not resemble this example; instead, they might suffer the fate of nineteenth-century horses, which have been completely pushed out of the job market today. Interestingly, even the opinion and taste of artificial intelligence are beginning to prevail over human preferences. This is something that has already happened with the Google search engine. Right now, those who design web pages often cater to the taste of Google's search algorithm, rather than to the taste of any other human. They look to see what Google says; for instance, even though Google's algorithm cannot taste any ice cream, the most successful ice cream sellers in the world are those who rank high in Google's search algorithm and appear first in searches, not necessarily those who produce the most delicious ice cream. So, with that in mind, what else will guarantee the physical survival and mental health of humans? Humanity must inevitably create new social and economic models as soon as possible, and these models must be guided by the principle of supporting humans, not job positions. For the unemployment crisis in the near future, a new model gaining more and more attention is universal basic income. Meaning that everyone has a fixed minimum salary. This action reduces the pressures caused by unemployment and economic instability for the poor. Another theory in this regard suggests that we should expand our definition of a job and change our mentality about work. For example, let's think that taking care of a child is definitely one of the most important and challenging jobs in the world. So, in that case, why would you call a mother who is at home taking care of and raising her child unemployed? She is also working and should have benefits. Perhaps this way we can solve part of the unemployment problem. But then the question arises: who determines the nature and extent of these newly recognized jobs, and who is going to pay for this work? Since six-month-old babies cannot pay their mothers a salary, perhaps governments should take on such a responsibility. Another option is for the government, instead of paying money to people, to support free education, free healthcare, free transportation, and basic needs. Universal basic support means prioritizing fundamental human needs. But another problem is that we do not have, and have never had, a widely accepted definition for basic services and basic needs. For instance, in medieval Europe, was access to church services more important as a basic need than access to food, or in today's world, is internet access a primary and basic need for everyone? So we must reach a global agreement on what exactly constitutes a basic need and what counts as a basic service. Note that when we talk about solutions to global problems in the near future, and discuss universal income, free education, free healthcare, and salaries for stay-at-home mothers, these things must be implemented globally to resolve issues, not just at the level of a specific country. Globalization has made the people of one country completely dependent on the markets of other countries. But can American voters, for example, accept that the taxes they pay be used to support the unemployed in African countries? The third lesson is about freedom and the challenges that threaten human freedom in the near future. For thousands of years, humans thought that authority originated from divine laws, not the human heart, and that we must sanctify the word of God, not human freedom; time passed, and the source of authority shifted only in these last few centuries from heavenly gods to flesh-and-blood humans, and the human became more important than anything else. But it seems authority is not destined to remain in human hands either. This time, authority may soon transfer from humans to algorithms . We are now at the intersection of two massive revolutions. On one hand, biologists are decoding the secrets of the body, especially the human brain and emotions, while on the other hand, computer scientists are providing us with unprecedented data processing power. When the biotech revolution merges with the data revolution, big data algorithms emerge that can monitor your emotions and mine, understand us better than we understand ourselves, and that is where authority will likely shift from humans to algorithms. Consider this example. The word television comes from the Greek "tele," meaning far, and "visio," meaning sight ; seeing from afar. Television generally refers to a device that allows us to see from a distance, but this same television will soon allow us to be seen from a distance. Just as George Orwell depicted in his novel 1984, when we watch television, it is as if the television is watching us, recording our cinematic interests. That is why it can subsequently select movies for us with amazing precision, and algorithms can suggest new movies based on what we watch, or new music based on what we listen to. That was just an example of film and music. In all other aspects of our lives, artificial intelligence has either already done this or will do so in the near future. Today we no longer look for information; we search on Google, and as we increasingly rely on Google to find answers, our ability to search for information independently diminishes. We learn through experience to trust Google, and after a year or two, we blindly trust whatever Google tells us. We currently listen to Netflix recommendations to choose movies, rely on Google Maps to tell us when to turn left or right, and gradually we will turn to AI to choose our fields of study, our workplaces, and even our spouses; and when power shifts from humans to algorithms, we become small chipsets within massive data processing systems. Some might say that algorithms can never make important decisions for us. Because important decisions usually have an ethical dimension, and algorithms have no understanding of ethics. But there is no reason to assume that in the near future, algorithms cannot act like an ordinary human, even in ethics. Besides , algorithms that are supposed to replace humans do not need to be perfect. They only need to be better than humans, and of course, it is we who teach algorithms what ethics means. So, it is possible that for some reason , we raise unethical algorithms. Consider this example. In a research study, a hypothetical scenario was presented to people in which a self-driving car with a single passenger in the backseat was about to crash, and to save the passenger's life , it would have to run over several people walking on the sidewalk. This self-driving car could be programmed in two ways. First, in that moment when it has to choose between the passenger's life and the lives of several pedestrians, it could save the passenger and take the pedestrians ' lives, or conversely, sacrifice the passenger for the sake of the pedestrians. The question asked of people was, how should this car act at that moment? Should we program the first solution or the second? Most people said that in such a situation, the car should save the pedestrians at the cost of the owner's life. Why? It's obvious, isn't it? Because the lives of several people are more valuable than the life of one passenger. But then, when they were asked if they would be willing to buy a car programmed to sacrifice its owner for something more valuable? That is where most said no. So, what reason would a car manufacturer have to program something that most people don't like and wouldn't buy? Now, what if this issue were optional? Imagine you have bought a new car that requires you to set some configurations before you can use it. In the event of an accident, do you want your car to sacrifice your life for a family in the adjacent car? Would you enable that setting? Probably not. This is where the government might need to intervene, apply market regulations, and implement a mandatory and unchangeable ethical code in all self-driving cars. Let's examine the next challenge with a real-life example . In March 1968, a group of American soldiers, who had been trapped for months in guerrilla warfare against the Vietnamese, became so nervous, exhausted, and enraged that they raided a village in South Vietnam called My Lai and massacred about 400 civilians. This massacre did not contribute to any strategic goals and was a major military and ethical violation. It could be said that if the U.S. had deployed robot soldiers in Vietnam, the My Lai massacre would never have happened. However, before we act hastily to create and deploy robot soldiers, we must remember that the behavior of robots is always a reflection of their code. If those codes are controlled and benevolent, the robots will naturally perform better; but if the codes are ruthless and cruel, the results will be catastrophic. The real problem with robots is not their artificial intelligence, but the natural stupidity and cruelty of their human masters. In the previous example about vehicle accidents, no car manufacturer would maliciously or heartlessly program their cars to attack people. However, there may be many corrupt governments that would love to have ruthless and unethical killer robot soldiers. For instance, what do you think the Kim regime in North Korea would do with robot soldier technology and AI technology in general? In the near future, every North Korean citizen will likely be required to wear a biometric bracelet so that the government can monitor all their behavior and speech, from their blood pressure to all brain activity and whatever each citizen is thinking about. By using increasing knowledge of the human brain and harnessing the immense power of AI, North Korea could, for the first time in history, know exactly what every single citizen is thinking at any given moment. If you look at a picture of the North Korean leader, the biometric sensors will start recording your neural signals and states, and if you even feel internally upset upon seeing the leader's photo, you will certainly end up in North Korea's notorious prisons. Dictators similar to the North Korean one might not be able to provide the free healthcare and basic services we discussed earlier. But these dictators can force people to love them from within, or else they will face severe consequences. It seems that even if democracy can adapt to the near-future world and AI developments and survive, people may still fall victim to a new kind of oppression and discrimination. Another issue is the risk of unfair judgment by algorithms. When you apply for a loan from a bank, for example, your application is reviewed by an algorithm rather than a human. If the bank rejects your loan application and you ask for the reasons , the bank's answer is that the algorithm said no. You ask, "Well, why? ""What is my problem?" You get the answer, "We don't know." No human understands such an algorithm. Because it functions based on hundreds of millions of data points it possesses, and we trust the algorithm, so we won't give you a loan. Pay attention: when discrimination is applied against a group, such as women or Black people, these groups can organize protests against that group-based discrimination . But today, an algorithm can discriminate against a specific individual, and the person discriminated against cannot figure out why, nor can they go out and protest alone. Perhaps the algorithm has been set in a way that it found something in your DNA, your personal history, or your Facebook and Instagram posts that it found unfavorable. Alongside these negative challenges, the good news is that it is unlikely that algorithms will become conscious or achieve sentience in the near future. Keep in mind that intelligence and consciousness are two completely different things. Intelligence is the ability to solve problems, but consciousness is the ability to feel, like pain, joy, love, or anger. Because our knowledge of consciousness is so minimal, it seems unlikely that we will be able to design conscious computers in the near future. That is why the use of artificial intelligence, despite its immense power, will remain more or less dependent on human consciousness for an unpredictable period of time. The danger is that if we put too much effort into transforming AI and relatively little into evolving human consciousness, the highly complex AI of computers might only serve to reinforce human stupidity; like the example of North Korea. If we look at history, we humans have bred cows that produce massive amounts of milk. But aside from that, these cows are much weaker than their ancestors, and their agility, curiosity, and environmental adaptability have significantly diminished. Now, the same thing could happen to humans. We are creating tame humans who produce vast amounts of data and act like highly efficient chips. But these data cows are not very active in upgrading or enhancing their own human capabilities. If we humans are not careful, we will turn into degraded beings who are exploited by evolved computers to lead themselves and the world around them to destruction. That is why we must ensure that the owners of data, who hold the real power, do not misuse our information. "Those Who Own Data Own the Future" is the headline of the fourth lesson of the book, and the title of the fourth lesson is Equality. This lesson gives a very brief explanation regarding inequality among humans and talks about the owners of data. In recent decades, people around the world have been told that humanity is on the path to equality and that globalization and new technologies will lead us to equality sooner. But the twenty-first century may actually be the age of the most unequal societies in history. Although globalization and the internet reduce the gap between countries, they deepen the class gap within them, and just when it seems humanity has achieved global unity, the human species is being divided into different biological classes within itself. At the beginning of the twenty-first century, people expected that, over time, the people of India and Egypt would enjoy similar opportunities and privileges to those of Finland and Canada; but evidence shows that this promise will not be fulfilled, because wealth and power are in the hands of a few rulers—those who own the data. If we want to prevent the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a few rulers, the way is to exert control over the ownership of data. The race for data acquisition has already begun, and data giants like Google, Facebook, and Baidu are at the forefront, with people helping these giants wittingly or unwittingly. Centuries ago, native African and American tribes unknowingly sold all their lands to European imperialists, receiving only colorful beads and decorative items in return. The same thing is happening right now, as people trade their most valuable asset—their personal data—to tech giants in exchange for free email services and entertaining videos. Perhaps it matters to you that your personal information goes to Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook instead of, say, the Russian intelligence services and Vladimir Putin. But you should know that the Cambridge Analytica firm in Britain demonstrated that any data entrusted to Zuckerberg can indirectly reach Putin as well. So, it seems there may not be much of a choice after all. Part one of the book has come to an end. As we mentioned, the first part of the book examined the current difficult technological situation and the dangers that technology brings us; now, in the second part, after outlining the challenges modern humans face, the author explores a wide range of potential and probable responses. The second part, titled "Political Challenges," also includes a header stating that any solution offered for these challenges must be global and incorporate international cooperation. Let's see what the first lesson in this section is. The first lesson, titled " Community"—which is the book's fifth lesson—discusses online and offline communities and provides an interesting example regarding Facebook. On March 16 , 2017, Mark Zuckerberg released a bold manifesto regarding the necessity of creating a global community and Facebook's role in this project. He explained that the turmoils of our time have largely led to the fragmentation of human communities, and people have become distanced from one another. Zuckerberg lamented that membership in various types of groups has declined by a quarter over the last few decades. He promised that Facebook would take on the task of leading the reconstruction of these communities, stating, "We are deploying tools that make building communities easier, and for this purpose, we have started building AI, which has been quite effective so far." Our ultimate goal is to help at least 1 billion people join meaningful communities. However, a few months after this important speech by Zuckerberg, and just as this book was being prepared for publication, it was revealed that the data entrusted to Facebook was being exploited by third-party actors—likely Russians— who used this information to manipulate and influence elections around the world. Setting this aside, even though the security dilemma has been called into question, it is still worth examining Facebook's vision to see if online social networks can help build global human communities. Facebook has achieved astonishing success in recent years and currently has about 2 billion online users. But if it wants to realize its new vision, it must bridge the deep gap between online and offline . Not everyone is online on Facebook all the time. If one day a dictator in their country wants to block access to Facebook or shut down the internet entirely, will those communities disappear? Are the people of that country capable of organizing protests without online communication? Another issue is that real-world communities have a depth that virtual communities lack, at least in the near future. If I get sick and am in bed at home, my online friends in California can talk to me and comfort me, but they can't make me soup. Despite knowing this, we are still more inclined to know what is happening in cyberspace than what is happening on the street. Talking to our online friends around the world is easier for us than talking to our spouse at the breakfast table. Because my dear spouse is buried in their phone instead of looking at me. We are becoming so absorbed in technology that we are losing our relationships and even ourselves. Humans have bodies, and technology over the last century has created a distance between us and our bodies. If you don't feel comfortable in your own skin, you can never feel good about your outer world. Now let's go back to Facebook. Can Facebook adopt a new model that encourages people to be online only when absolutely necessary and to dedicate more attention to their real-world relationships, their bodies, and their feelings? If it does this, it is essentially saying, "People, come to virtual Facebook less and be more in real, offline relationships," and well, that is to Facebook's detriment. Facebook's ultimate test will be when an engineer creates a tool that causes people to spend less time online and engage more in offline activities with their friends. Will Facebook support such a tool, or will it ban it? Will there be a leap in Facebook's beliefs, and will Facebook prioritize social considerations over financial interests ? If it does that and then manages to survive bankruptcy, that is when it will have undergone a massive transformation. Well, that was lesson five, which was about community. Lessons six and seven of the book are about civilization and nationalism, which we will review together because they have many common points and are among the most fascinating sections of the book. So pay close attention. Humanity has always been divided into various civilizations, where people of each civilization viewed the world differently, and this very different view of the world has been the source of conflicts between civilizations— the source of wars. Given that all of humanity in the contemporary era forms a single civilization, and considering that humanity faces common challenges, then why are the British, Americans, Russians, and many others turning toward nationalist isolation? Does the turn toward nationalism provide us with real solutions to the world's unprecedented problems? Or is it a comforting delusion that could lead humanity and the entire biosphere to destruction? To answer this question, we must first cast aside a misconception that is deeply ingrained in our minds. That is, contrary to popular belief, nationalism is not a natural and eternal part of the human psyche, and it has no roots in biology. The reality is that when humans in their small tribes could no longer respond to the challenges they faced, they eventually decided to form larger national communities to overcome bigger problems together, and that is where national societies were formed. Consider the examples of the ancient tribes that lived along the Nile River thousands of years ago. The Nile was their lifeblood. It irrigated their fields and transported their trade goods from place to place. But the Nile also had major problems. Too little rain meant famine and death, and too much rain was synonymous with the river flooding and destroying entire villages . No single tribe could solve this problem on its own. Because each tribe controlled only a small part of the river and was unable to mobilize more than a few hundred workers. Only through a joint effort to build massive dams and dig hundreds of kilometers of canals could there be hope of taming and harnessing the Nile, and this was one of the important reasons why tribes gradually merged into a single nation. Such a nation had the ability to build dams and canals and was able to bring the river's flow under control and overcome a major challenge that small tribes could not handle. So national communities were formed, each one grew larger and larger, and human culture took shape within the societies they lived in, and national identity found meaning. Up to this point, there is no problem. The issue with national identity and patriotism arises when I believe that my nation is unique and that I have obligations and commitments to my fellow citizens that force me to prioritize them excessively and make sacrifices for them. The problem appears when a mild patriotism turns into an extreme nationalism, and extreme nationalism brings with it war and slaughter. The concept of nationalism, which was a human invention and had no roots in biology, nature, or the human psyche, remained very attractive and popular until the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. But World War II changed everything. The invention of nuclear weapons disrupted the balance of nationalistic arrangements. After the Hiroshima incident, the fear of nationalistic wars gave way to a greater fear called the fear of nuclear war. A war that can destroy everyone, and not just one specific country. The problems of nuclear war cannot be solved through nationalism, and humanity must combat this dilemma within a global community that transcends borders. Just as ancient villagers along the Nile shifted their loyalty from local tribes to great national kings, enabling them to tame the river's dangers. In the nuclear age , a global community also gradually emerged above various nations. Because only such a community could contain the nuclear demon. Consequently, nationalism retreated during the Cold War, and when the Cold War ended, globalization emerged for the future. Fanatical nationalists who cry "my country first" must ask themselves whether their nation, alone and without a robust system of international cooperation, is capable of protecting the world or even itself from nuclear threats. The next major issue is the great environmental crisis. Since 1945, most countries no longer use war as a conventional political tool. Despite wars in Syria, Ukraine, and a few other hotspots, the cause of human casualties has been obesity, traffic accidents, or suicide more than human violence in war , and this is perhaps the greatest political and moral achievement of our era. But this does not mean that things are going well. In the coming decades, humanity will face a new threat to its survival that has an even higher priority than atomic and nuclear war. A threat called environmental collapse. Humans are destroying the overall balance of the planet on multiple fronts. We take ever more resources from the environment and, in return, dump terrifying amounts of waste and toxins into it, thereby transforming the composition of soil, water, and air . Animal habitats are destroyed by agricultural activities, resulting in the extinction of the region's plants and animals. Homo sapiens has acted as an ecological serial killer for thousands of years and has now become an agent of mass ecological slaughter. If the current trend continues, we will not only face the destruction of various life forms on a massive scale, but the foundation of human civilization will also be destroyed. Scientific estimates show that if we do not significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions over the next 20 years, the Earth's average temperature will rise by more than 2 degrees Celsius, leading to the expansion of deserts, the destruction of glaciers, rising ocean levels, and extreme weather events like storms and hurricanes. These changes, in turn, will cause agricultural production to cease and cities to be submerged. Huge parts of the world will become uninhabitable, and all this will lead to the migration of hundreds of millions of refugees in search of a place to live. Given this great threat, does nationalism have an answer to the environmental threat? Is there any nation now, no matter how powerful, that can stop global warming on its own ? Certainly not. This problem requires global and cross-border measures. Another interesting example in the book is about the meat industry. Currently, the meat industry not only causes suffering and torture for billions of creatures that feel and sense pain, but it is also a key driver of global warming. This industry is one of the main consumers of antibiotics and toxins, and one of the largest polluters of air, land, and water. According to a report by the Institute of Mechanical Engineers, producing one kilogram of beef requires 15,000 liters of water. But what if engineers find a way to produce meat through cell culture? If you want a burger, you just need to culture the burger and skip raising and slaughtering an entire cow. This might seem like science fiction now, but in 2013, the first cell-cultured burger was produced and consumed. Its price was 330,000 dollars . Four years of research and development brought this price down to 11 dollars per burger, and it is expected that in the next decade, industrial meat production will become cheaper than slaughtered meat. This technical transformation could save billions of animals from a miserable life, help save billions of humans suffering from malnutrition from hunger , and simultaneously prevent environmental collapse to some extent. So this major problem is solvable, but effective action must be taken at a global level. Preventing environmental threats requires cooperation from all the people of the world. If one country reduces its greenhouse gas emissions to zero, but several other countries pay no attention to the issue, that single country's action is ineffective. Nationalistic isolationism regarding climate change may be even more dangerous than in the context of nuclear war. In an all-out nuclear war, all nations are doomed to destruction. So all nations have an equal stake in preventing it. But global warming may have a different impact on different nations. Some countries, especially Russia, might actually benefit from it. Russia has few coastlines. Therefore, it has much less concern about rising sea levels than China. Meanwhile, higher temperatures might even turn Siberia into a fertile region. Furthermore, when the ice in Siberia melts, the Arctic seas under Russian control may become a global trade artery. Likewise, to replace fossil fuels with renewable energy sources, China, Japan, and South Korea, which depend on massive imports of oil and gas, might be very pleased. But Russia, Iran, and Saudi Arabia, which depend on oil and gas exports, might not be inclined toward this. What is the nationalistic response to these threats ? There is no nationalistic response. Humanity may need a kind of global identity and loyalty. If we want to make wise choices about the future of human life, we must go beyond a nationalist vision and view issues from a global and even planetary perspective . We need a new global identity because national institutions lack the capability to solve global problems. A person can simultaneously be loyal to their family, their neighbors, and their nation. Up to this point, the focus has been on the national circle and the country. But why not add humanity and planet Earth to this list? Yes, an individual can simultaneously be loyal to and feel responsible for their family, neighbors, nation, fellow humans, and all beings on planet Earth. Well, that is it for the topic of nationalism. The next lesson in the book and the next subject is about religion. This part begins with the fundamental question: to what extent are religions compatible with our current situation? Can they help us solve the major problems we are facing? To understand the role of traditional religions in the 21 st-century world, we must distinguish between three types of problems. The first is technical problems. For example, how should farmers in drought-stricken countries cope with drought caused by global warming? The second is policy-making problems. For instance, what criteria should governments prioritize to prevent global warming? The third is identity problems. For example, should I care about the problems of farmers on the other side of the world, or is it enough to dedicate myself to the problems of my own tribe and country? Let's first address technical problems and see what help religion can offer in this area. In the past, when an agricultural crisis occurred due to drought or locust swarms, farmers would turn to priests to pray for them so the problem would be solved. Priests were intermediaries between them and the gods. Furthermore, medicine also fell within the religious domain. Almost every prophet was both a spiritual leader and a healer. That is why Christ spent a lot of time healing the sick, giving sight to the blind, and curing the insane. However, in recent times, biologists and surgeons have replaced priests and miracle workers. If the child of a devout Hindu gets a severe illness, the father prays before the Hindu gods and offers flowers and sweets at the local temple, but he immediately takes the child to the hospital and puts them in the hands of doctors. In reality, the true expertise of priests and spiritual teachers has never actually been healing, prophecy, or magic. A priest is someone who can justify droughts and floods and knows why we should continue to believe in God. A priest cannot prescribe medicine or make crops grow more. But they can provide a reason for droughts and floods. Medicine, prescriptions, and research are the work of scientists. So , the first set of problems can be solved better by scientists than by priests. The second set of problems involved adopting appropriate policies. For instance, what criteria should governments prioritize to prevent global warming? Although science leads us to clear answers for technical questions like curing measles. Yet, for example, regarding the choice of the right policy to combat global warming, there is significant disagreement among scientists. Almost all scientists agree that global warming is a reality. But there is no consensus on the best response to this threat. Now, can religions help here? At first glance, we might say religions are old and the problems are new, but religions can update themselves. In the 1970s, Latin American theologians did just this, imagining Jesus Christ somewhat like Che Guevara. Similarly, later on, Christ was able to simply enter the debate about global warming as well. However, even if priests can find passages in different parts of the Bible to support their position, the real source for solving the dilemma remains scientific and political opinions, not the Bible. From this perspective, religion cannot really contribute much to the major policy debates of our time. The third type of problems were identity issues, where perhaps religions can help people. We previously said that in the twenty-first century, religions cannot cure diseases or build bombs, but in their own way, they can explain who we are, who we should heal, and whom we should drop bombs on. Today, many countries, while utilizing global tools and modern structures, simultaneously rely on traditional religions to create a national identity. In some cases, governments have even created an entirely new religion to reinforce their unified identity. The best contemporary example could be North Korea, the former Japanese colony. The North Korean regime mesmerizes its masses with a fanatical new state religion called "Juche," which is a mixture of Marxism-Leninism, some ancient Korean traditions, a racist belief in the unique purity of the Korean race, and the deification of the Kim Il-sung family. In the "Rokh" podcast, in the "North Korea" episode, we talked about them in detail; anyway. Religions still hold significant political power, to the extent that they can create national identities and even ignite the flames of a third world war. Although many traditional religions embrace universal values and claim cosmic validity, they are currently used primarily as fodder for modern nationalism. What does that mean ? It means, for example, when we address issues related to global warming or nuclear proliferation, Jewish rabbis encourage Israelis to focus primarily on what is in the interest of Israel and Judaism. Orthodox priests urge Russians to prioritize the interests of Russia and Orthodox Christianity above all else, while Islamic leaders in Muslim countries also pursue their own interests, each holding the view that they are God’s chosen people or faith , and therefore whatever benefits their own group must also please and satisfy God. This is happening while humanity is in need of a unified civilization, and problems like nuclear war and environmental collapse can only be solved on a global scale. One of the most important current challenges ahead of us is the heated debate over migration, and the book's ninth lesson covers this very topic. Migration. To clarify the issue, we will examine migration as a contract with three basic conditions. The first condition is that the host allows immigrants to enter. The second condition is that, in return, immigrants must at least accept the norms and core values of the host country. Even if this means letting go of some of their own traditional norms and values. The third condition is that if immigrants integrate sufficiently, they will eventually become members of the host country with equal rights; meaning "they" become "us." Let us consider these three basic conditions for migration and briefly discuss each one. The first clause of the migration contract states that the host should allow immigrants to enter; but is this a duty or a favor? Proponents of migration believe that countries have a moral duty to accept not only refugees but also people from very poor countries who are searching for work and a better future. They believe that in a unified world, all humans have moral obligations toward one another, and those who lack such a sense of responsibility are selfish and even racist. Conversely, opponents of migration believe that one of the most fundamental rights of any human collective, whether it is an army or a society of immigrants, is to protect itself against encroachment. So with this view, if Swedish voters choose that they do not want any more Syrian immigrants, it is their right to prevent their entry; and if Swedes do accept them, it should be seen strictly as a sign of their favor. What complicates the matter is that in many cases, people want to have their cake and eat it too! There are many countries that do not show sensitivity toward illegal immigrants, or even accept foreign workers on a temporary basis. Why? Because they want to make use of cheap labor. But then, when you tell them that these illegal immigrants who are working and toiling should be able to migrate legally and have citizenship rights, These people say, " No, we don't want immigrants." To give an example outside of the book, exactly what is happening in Iran regarding Afghan immigrants is just this. We are utilizing the cheap labor of Afghans in all fields, but at the same time, we say we do not want Afghan immigrants. This issue could lead to hierarchical societies in the long run, where the upper classes have full citizenship rights and exploit foreign immigrants. Just as they are already doing in Qatar , Dubai, and many other countries. That covers the discussion regarding the first condition of migration. The second condition of migration stated that if immigrants are accepted, they are obligated to integrate into the local culture. But what are the limits of this integration? If immigrants come from a deeply religious country, are they required to adopt a secular worldview? Must they abandon their traditional patterns of dress and their own judicial taboos? Pro-migration advocates believe, for example, that immigrants to Europe should not be forced to conform to a European identity. They believe that if Europe has something called a value, that value is its freedom. Therefore, immigrants should also have the right to choose and be free in all areas. In contrast, opponents of migration accept that freedom is one of Europe's most important values. However, they accuse immigrants of being the ones who are actually calling this very freedom into question. They say immigrants are misogynistic. They exert power over their families, are extremist in religion, and if Europe continues to take in immigrants from the Middle East , Europe will soon become a second Middle East. This is a complex debate, and perhaps part of this problem could be solved if immigrants show that in their views on gender and politics, they are liberal and broad-minded, and not as the opponents claim. And now the third discussion; the third clause of the migration contract stated that if immigrants make a sincere effort to integrate, the host country commits to accepting them as first-class citizens. But the question is, exactly when is it necessary for immigrants to be recognized as true members of society? Should first-generation Algerian immigrants feel uncomfortable if, after 20 years of living in France, they are not recognized as fully French? Or what about third-generation immigrants whose grandparents came to France in the 1970s? Are they still immigrants, or should they be considered first-class citizens after three generations? Pro-migration advocates expect immigrants to be quickly accepted as citizens. While opponents of migration demand a very long probationary period. The main problem in this debate is the gap between personal timing and collective timing. From the perspective of a collective outlook, 40 years is a very short time. Full acceptance of foreign groups by a society within a few decades is an unreasonable expectation. Past civilizations that accepted foreigners as equal citizens, such as the Roman Empire, the Islamic Caliphate, the Chinese Empire, and the United States, all needed centuries, not decades, to accomplish this transformation. But well, this same 40 years from an individual's perspective can be a lifetime. For a teenager born in France after their father immigrated from Algeria, who speaks French instead of Arabic and has never even seen Algeria, France is the only home they know; and 40 years is a very long time to wait for acceptance. Now, we have raised these three discussions and challenges; but above all these disagreements regarding the precise definition of the immigration contract, the final question is whether both sides are actually committed to their obligations in immigration or not? Do they even intend to fulfill those three conditions at all? Opponents of immigration argue that immigrants do not fulfill the conditions of the second point. Meaning they do not make a sincere effort to integrate, and many of them hold regressive views. Therefore, the host country has no reason to fulfill the third point, which is recognizing them as equal citizens. In response, proponents of immigration reply that it is the host country that is failing to fulfill its commitment to the contract. Host countries, despite the sincere efforts of the vast majority of immigrants, make integration conditions difficult, and worse yet, they continue to treat even second and third-generation immigrants who have successfully integrated as second-class citizens. The next subtle point is this: if 1 million immigrants are law-abiding citizens, but 100 people join terrorist groups and attack the host country, does this mean that the entire immigrant population has not adhered to the contract and has violated it? Conversely, if an immigrant crosses a street 100 times without being harassed , but is attacked by a racist once... does this mean that the natives have not accepted the immigrants? In discussing and concluding the issue of immigration, we must be very mindful of these points as well. But hidden beneath all these discussions is a much more fundamental question related to our understanding of human culture. The question is, is it possible, for instance, when Germans are debating the admission of 1 million Syrian refugees, that they are justified in thinking that German culture is somehow better than Syrian culture? To put it simply, does a German have the right to think their culture is superior to Syrian culture or not? To answer this question , let's take a look at the past. 100 years ago, Europeans took it for granted that some races, specifically the white race, were inherently superior to other races. Later, after World War II and the defeat of the fascists, racism was condemned and portrayed as morally horrific. However, over time, racism gave way to culturalism. With a few differences. Traditional racism was strongly based on biological theories. In the early twentieth century, it was widely believed in countries like Britain, Australia, and the US that certain inherited biological traits made Africans and Chinese people less intelligent, less innovative, and morally inferior to Europeans. As if the problem were in their blood. Those theories once held significant political and scientific credibility, but as science advanced, they lost their validity, and this time, proponents turned to culture. The era of claiming that Black people commit crimes due to defective genes is over, but instead, it is now claimed that they commit crimes because they belong to dysfunctional and inferior cultures. The unfortunate part is that, previously, racists could not blame Black people for failing to turn their skin white. But culturalists can accuse Africans or Muslims of failing to adopt Western cultural norms and values, and they do just that. Many culturalist claims have three major flaws. The first flaw is that culturalists often mistake local superiority for objective superiority. This means that if a region is doing better, it does not necessarily mean its culture is better. I will explain the second flaw with an example. For instance, saying that Islamic culture is very violent is a very vague claim. Because we must first define what is meant by Islamic culture . Is it the Arabian Peninsula at the dawn of Islam in the eighth century? Is it the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century? Is it Pakistan and Afghanistan at the beginning of the twenty-first century? What is the standard for this claim anyway? If we compare the sixteenth-century Ottoman Empire with sixteenth-century Western Europe, we conclude that Islamic culture is not violent compared to Western European culture; in fact, Western European culture was more violent. If we move forward and compare Afghanistan under the Taliban with, say, present-day Switzerland, we reach a different result. So, one cannot speak in such general terms. But the third and biggest problem with culturalist claims is that they often rely on prejudging individuals. For example, because someone is migrating from Iran to a European country, it is assumed that since they are Iranian, they must be Muslim, and therefore all the flaws I attribute to Muslims in my mind must exist in this person as well. Overall, the debate about migration is a debate between two legitimate political positions that should be resolved through conventional democratic procedures and should not turn into an irreconcilable conflict. If 500 million affluent Europeans cannot integrate a few million poor and desperate refugees , then there is no hope left for humanity to overcome the greater problems of the global community.

۲

پادکست رخ · مدت ۱:۲۲:۵۳ · دیدن در یوتیوب
خلاصهجای خالی

۰:۰۰دوستان سلام شما به دومین و آخرین قسمت از خلاصه کتاب بیست و یک درس برای قرن بیست و یکم گوش میکنید اثری ماندگار و پرمغز از نویسنده مشهوری به نام یواال نوح هراری امیدوارم که اپیزود اول رو دوست داشته باشید و از مطالب اپیزود دوم هم لذت ببرید این کتاب همونطور که از اسمش مشخصه بیست و یک درس داره که در اپیزود اول ما 9 درس رو با هم مرور کردیم این 21 درس در قالب 5 بخش بودن که دو بخش اول رو در اپیزود اول روایت کردیم بخش اول کتاب با عنوان چالش های فنی با بررسی وضعیت دشوار سیاسی و فنی جاری دنیا شروع شد و در ادامه به خطراتی که فن آوری برای ما به ارمغان میاره پرداخت درس های سرخوردگی از حکومت های لیبرال معضلات کار در آینده نزدیک و مفاهیم آزادی و برابری در این بخش بررسی شدن

۰:۵۸در بخش دوم با عنوان چالش سیاسی بعد از طرح چالش هایی که انسان امروزی باهاش مواجهه یه پهنه وسیعی از پاسخ های بالقوه و احتمالی بررسی شد درس های اجتماع آنلاین و آفلاین و مفاهیم تمدن و ناسیونالیسم و دین و در انتها معضل مهاجرت هم در این بخش بررسی شدن حالا در بخش سوم با عنوان نا امیدی و امید خواهیم دید که اگرچه چالش های بی سابقه و بزرگی در مقابل ما قرار داره و اختلافات سیاسی شدیدی بر جهان حاکمه اما اگر بشر بتواند بر ترس های خودش غلبه کنه و موضع متواضعانه تری نسبت به نظراتش اختیار کنه میتونه فرصت های بیشتری هم به دست بیاره و موقعیت بهتری برای خودش ترسیم کنه یکی از ترس هایی که انسان امروزی باهاش مواجهه ترس از تروریسمه که موضوع درس دهم هم همینه موضوع تروریسمه

۱:۵۲با یک جمله که در کنارش نوشته شده وحشت نکن بریم ببینیم این درس برای ما چی داره تروریست ها استاد کنترل بر ذهن ها هستن آنها افراد معدودی را می کشند اما با این حال بر وجود میلیاردها انسان وحشت میندازن و ساختارهای عظیمی چون پیمان اروپا و ای لات متحده را به لرزه درمیارن یک سکه کوچک در یک سطل بزرگ خالی صدای زیادی به راه می اندازد این همان چیزیه که نمایش تروریسم را موفقیت آمیز نشون میده تروریسم یک استراتژی نظامیه که امیدواره تا وضعیت سیاسی را با ایجاد وحشت تغییر بده در مقابل حکومت ها هم در پاسخ به نمایش تروریست ها

۲:۵۰برای بازگردوندن آرامش مردم نمایش های پرشکوه امنیتی و قدرتی تدارک میبینن مثلا اقدام به کشتار جمعی بزرگتری میکنن یا کشورهای خارجی رو اشغال میکنن چنین واکنش غلوآمیزی نسبت به تروریسم در اکثر موارد خطرات بسیار بزرگ تر از خطرات تروریستی علیه امنیت عمومی به وجود میاره و اصلا واکنش مناسبی نیست مؤثرترین پاسخ به تروریسم می تواند هشیاری ب لا و مقابله غیر علنی با شبکه های مالی تغذیه کننده تروریسم باشد اما این چیزی نیست که شهروندان بتوانند تو تلویزیون ببینن و راضی بشن و دلشون خنک بشه شهروندان نمایش فروریختن مرکز تجاری ایالت متحده را در 11 سپتامبر دیدن و دولت احساس میکنه که ناچاره با یک نمایش بزرگتر پا به صحنه بگذارد

۳:۴۷حتی با دود و آتش بیشتر بنابراین به جای یک حرکت آرام و حساب شده توفان مهیبی به پا میکند که این واکنش معمولا دلخواًه ترین آرزوهای تروریست ها را برآورده می کند چیزی که تروریست ها میخوان اینه که ذهن ما رو احاطه کنن ماحملات تروریستی رو بارها و بارها در صحنه ذهن خودمون مرور میکنیم تروریست ها صد نفر رو میکشن و باعث میشن صد میلیون نفر تصور کنن که در پشت هر درختی یک تروریست کمین کرده برای مقابله با تروریسم وظیفه هر شهروندی اینه که ذهنش رو از تروریست ها پاک کنه و واکنشی نداشته باشه که رسانه ها رو وادار کنه که اونا هم در تروریسم غرق بشن و در نهایت دولت رو مجبور به واکنش های غیراصولی کنن تروریست ها به هیچ وجه اون جوری که ما فکر می کنیم قدرتمند و قوی نیستن

۴:۴۲موفقیت یا شکست تروریسم به ما بستگی دارد اگر ما به خودمون اجازه بدیم تا تخیلات ما توسط تروریست ها احاطه بشه و نسبت به ترس واکنش افراطی نشان بدیم اونوقته که تروریسم موفق میشه به چیزی که میخواد برسه اگر تخیلات و ذهن خودمون را از تروریست ها آزاد کنیم و برخوردی متعادل و خونسردانه داشته باشیم اون وقته که تروریسم شکست میخوره منتهی درحالی که تروریسم کنونی بیش از هر چیز یک شو یا نمایشه ولی تروریسم هسته ای آینده تروریسم سایبری یا تروریسم زیستی اینا دیگه صرفا نمایش نیستن و تهدیدات بسیار گسترده ای را به وجود می آورند که مقابله باهاشون مستلزم واکنش یکپارچه ای از جانب دولت ها با هم و در کنار هم خواهد بود ولی اگه برگردیم به حال

۵:۴۱احساس خطر کنونی ما بیشتر از این که به تروریسم مربوط بشه به ترس آدم ها از اتفاق وحشتناک و بزرگی به نام جنگ برمیگرده خیلی از متخصصین و مردم عادی از این می ترسند که تروریسم بهونه ای برای یه جنگ بزرگ باشه و جنگ جهانی _مثل صد سال پیش_ جایی در همین نزدیکی ها باشه به نظر می رسد که تنش های فزاینده میان قدرت های بزرگ به همراه مشکلات بغرنج جهانی شبیه به آن طور که در سال 1914 یعنی سال شروع جنگ جهانی دوم شاهدش بودیم داره ما را به سمت یک جنگ جهانی دیگه میکشونه برای همین درس بعدی راجع به جنگه عنوان درس بعدی جنگه و این جمله هم در کنارش نوشته شده حماقت بشر را هرگز دست کم نگیرید واقعیت اینه که

۶:۳۶دهه های اخیر صلح آمیزترین دوران در تاریخ بشر بوده امروز تنها یک درصد از مردم در اثر خشونت انسانی می میرند در حالی که این رقم در قرن بیستم ۵ درصد و در جوامع کشاورزی اولیه ۱۵ درصد بوده اما بعد از بحران مالی جهانی سال ۲۰۰۸ وضعیت جامعه بین الملل وخیم شد ایده های جنگ طلبی دوباره مطرح شد و مخارج نظامی سر به فلک زد مردم عادی و متخصصین از این می ترسند که همان طور که قتل ولیعهد اتریش در ۱۹۱۴ آتش جنگ جهانی اول رو روشن کرد در حال حاضر هم حادثه ای در بیابان های سوریه یا حرکت نسنجیده ای در شبه جزیره کره بیاد وآتش اختلافات جهانی را شعله ور کند اما خب چند تفاوت کلیدی بین دوران حاضر و سال ۱۹۱۴ وجود دارد

۷:۳۵در 1914 تمایل زیادی برای جنگ در بین حاکمان سراسر دنیا وجود داشت چون اونها فکر میکردن که جنگ میتونه باعث رونق اقتصاد و افزایش قدرت سیاسی بشه اما در حال حاضر به نظر میرسه که جنگ یک پدیده رو به انقراض باشد تا اونجا که حتی بزرگ ترین پیروزی در اذهان زنده یعنی پیروزی آمریکا بر اتحاد شوروی در جنگ سرد بدون هیچ درگیری وسیع نظامی به دست آمد بعد از اون تا به امروز تنها مورد اشغال موفقیت آمیز با کمک یک نیروی بزرگ نظامی در قرن بیست و یکم تسخیر کریمه توسط. روسیه بوده روسیه بدون جنگ چندانی سرزمینی را که از نظر استراتژیک ارزش حیاتی براش داشت رو تصرف کرد اما وقتی روسیه تلاش کرد تا موفقیتش در کریمه را در سایر نقاط شرقی اوکراین تکرار کند

۸:۳۲با مقاومت سخت تری مواجه شد و جنگ اوکراین براش شد یک باتلاق کشنده بدتر این بود که جنگ موجب برانگیختن احساسات ضد روسی در اوکراین شد و این کشور را از مقام متحد به یه دشمن قسم خورده تنزل داد اگر همه جنگ های روسیه در قفقاز و اوکراین رو در ابتدای قرن بیست و یکم حساب کنیم به سختی می توانیم آنها را موفقیت آمیز توصیف کنیم این جنگ ها اگرچه منزلت روسیه را به عنوان یک قدرت بزرگ تقویت کردند اما بی اعتمادی و خصومت نسبت به این کشور را در جهان افزایش داد برای درک ضعف های سیاست روسیه فقط کافیه که پیشرفت های عظیم صلح جویانه چین در بیست سال اخیر را با رکود روسیه طی همین دوره مقایسه کنیم روسیه 150 میلیون نفر جمعیت دارد

۹:۲۹و تولید ناخالص ملی اش به 4 تریلیون دلار می رسد و چه به لحاظ جمعیت و چه تولید در مقابل آمریکا با 325 میلیون جمعیت و 19 تریلیون دلار تولید و البته پیمان اروپا با 500 میلیون جمعیت و 21 تریلیون دلار تولید قطعا کم میاره جمعیت آمریکا و پیمان اروپا روی هم پنج برابر بیشتر از روسیه است و درامدشون ده برابر بیشتر موضوع مهم تر اینه که روسیه پوتین فاقد یک ایدئولوژی جهانیه اتحاد شوروی طی دوران جنگ سرد بر ایدئولوژی کمونیسم و ارتش سرخ جهانی استوار بود اما پوتینیسم بر خلاف آن دوران چیز زیادی ندارد تا به کوبایی ها، ویتنامی ها یا روشنفکران فرانسوی بده و اونا رو تو تیم خودش داشته باشه پس در قرن 21 جنگ برای قدرت های بزرگ انتخابیه که موفقیت در اون بسیار مشکله
